title: A 26-year-old father of three died alone in a cell at the Barton Street jail. More than four years later, his family now knows why
subtitle: Jury makes recommendations for change at Zakery Rogers inquest.
article: Zakery Rogers' family has for years wondered why the father of three died alone in a jail cell at the Hamilton-Wentworth Detention Centre.
They now have an answer.

Following a weeklong inquest that heard from correctional officers, doctors, forensic pathologists and family, a jury on Friday ruled the 26-year-old died as a result of myocarditis that had gone undetected by doctors.
Just before his death on Jan. 31, 2021, Rogers was under physician and nurse care at Hamilton General Hospital, being treated for cardiac arrest he had suffered two days earlier.

Doctors believed the cardiac arrest was induced by illicit drugs due to information from correctional officers as well as Rogers' history of substance use, the inquest heard. They felt it was appropriate to discharge him given his quick recovery and positive tests results - including ECGs that showed no signs of a heart attack.
When Rogers got back to the Barton jail, he was placed in an isolation cell, where staff monitor inmates suspected of hiding contraband.
Officers reported he appeared to be asleep when they checked his cell between 4:30 and 5:30 p.m.
On final check, Rogers was found without vitals and rushed to the same hospital he had been at hours earlier, The Spectator previously reported.
Staff at Hamilton General pronounced him dead at 6:34 p.m.
Among the tasks before the inquest jury was answering how Rogers died, if his death could have been prevented, and what steps hospitals and jails can take to avoid similar future outcomes.
An autopsy conducted days after Rogers died ruled the cause of death was inconclusive.

The inquest heard the initial post-mortem examined Rogers' heart but made no findings of disease. While the autopsy report was peer reviewed, it didn't include an independent exam of microscopic slides.
Four years later, a second look at the slides revealed widespread but subtle inflammation of Rogers' heart, according to Ontario's chief forensic pathologist.

Dr. Michael Pollanen, who conducted the second exam with an independent cardiac pathologist, testified the cause of death was myocarditis. The inquest heard Rogers had two cardiac arrests in 36 hours - the latter being fatal.

In her closing statement, inquest counsel Kristin Smith noted the two HGH doctors who saw Rogers before he was discharged testified they "couldn't disagree that there was heart muscle inflammation" in the second review. She said they both agreed Rogers had "some degree of myocarditis," and added one doctor "testified, 'There is no doubt. Pathology has demonstrated that.'"

The doctors testified that Rogers' clinical presentation did not support severe myocarditis. Pollanen noted in a report given to the jury that it was difficult for him "to take issue" with the clinicians and pathologists involved in the case.
"Some cases have complexities that are formidable challenges to diagnosis ... This is such a case."
The inquest heard staff at the Barton jail also weren't made aware of any possible heart issues with Rogers.

Among the 13 recommendations made by the jury to prevent future similar deaths was the creation of a committee between Hamilton Health Sciences (HHS) and the jail's health-care staff, which will include discharge instructions to better support people upon their return to jail. The jury further recommended that additional or updated training be offered to hospital and jail health-care staff on biases toward prisoners with a history of substance use.
Four of the 13 recommendations were aimed at HHS and the Ministry of the Solicitor General, while the remaining involved only the ministry.

The jury asked the ministry to consider upgrading CCTV cameras in the jail to record audio and remind correctional officers that checks on cells must include a verbal and visual confirmation of the inmate.

For inmates who are discharged from hospital, the jury recommended HWDC health-care staff take their vital signs every four hours for at least 24 hours after their return. The jury also suggested that discharge areas in jails include a poster with a phone number that people can call post-release to obtain a prescription or supply of their medication on short notice.

Rogers was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and manic depression following an arrest in early 2020. He was doing well on his medication, so his sister, Kylee Rogers, agreed to be his surety and helped him get bail. But after being released from Maplehurst Correctional Complex in Milton that Christmas Eve, her brother's prescriptions weren't accessible over the holidays. He then spiralled and ran away around New Year's Eve.
When Rogers got arrested again a month later, Kylee thought her brother was going to get the help he needed.
Instead, she got a call saying he had died.

On Friday, Kylee spoke to the jury about the aftermath of her brother's death. Part of her struggles over the last four years were due to what she knew - that her loving brother, with dreams and a life ahead of him, was no longer around. But just as difficult was what she didn't know.

"I can't tell you how difficult it has been not knowing and wondering what happened to my brother," she said during closing remarks. "Now I know he was suffering in a jail cell alone, his heart failing him, his lung becoming congested with fluid. This is a vision that haunts me every night when I close my eyes."
Kylee said she hoped the inquest would bring about meaningful change, spare other families the same pain and ensure more safeguards are in place to ensure people don't fall through the cracks.
